requirements: Reproduce the core contributions of FlashAttention-3 on Hopper H100 GPUs: warp-specialized producer-consumer asynchrony, GEMM-softmax pipelining, and FP8 attention with block quantization plus incoherent processing, matching reported speed and accuracy results.

sub_tasks.requirements: The Hopper H100 SXM5 build environment (CUDA 12.3, cuDNN 9.1.1.17, CUTLASS 3.5, FlashAttention 2.5.8, Triton nightly, PyTorch 2.3.0) is available and the GPU is locked to the reported 1830 MHz clock for reproducible benchmarking.
GPU hardware is available and identified as an NVIDIA H100 SXM5 (80 GB) accelerator with the correct compute capability.

Code has been implemented that detects the GPU model via `nvidia-smi` (or `torch.cuda.get_device_name`) and refuses to run the benchmarks unless the reported device is `H100 80GB HBM3` / `H100 SXM5` with compute capability 9.0.

Code has been implemented that emits a startup log line recording detected GPU name, driver version, total memory (must be ≥80 GiB) and SM count (expected 132) so downstream artifacts prove the H100 SXM5 was used.
The reported CUDA, cuDNN, and CUTLASS toolchain versions are installed and used to build the FlashAttention-3 kernel.
Code has been implemented that verifies CUDA toolkit version 12.3 is present (e.g. `nvcc --version` matches `release 12.3`) before compiling any kernel; a mismatch aborts the build.

Code has been implemented that verifies the installed cuDNN library version is 9.1.1.17 (checked via `libcudnn.so.9.1.1` symlink or `cudnnGetVersion`) so the cuDNN attention baseline is the version reported in the paper.

Code has been implemented that pins the CUTLASS submodule/dependency to tag/commit corresponding to release 3.5 and the kernel build includes CUTLASS 3.5 headers (grep for `#define CUTLASS_MAJOR 3` and `CUTLASS_MINOR 5` in the resolved include path).
The Python-side dependencies (PyTorch 2.3.0, FlashAttention 2.5.8, Triton nightly, plus the FA3 kernel binding) are pinned to the versions used in the paper.

Code has been implemented (e.g. `requirements.txt`, `environment.yml`, or setup script) that pins `torch==2.3.0` with a CUDA 12.x wheel; `import torch; torch.__version__` in the benchmark process returns `2.3.0` and `torch.version.cuda` starts with `12.`.
Code has been implemented that installs `flash-attn==2.5.8` as the FlashAttention-2 baseline (verified by `flash_attn.__version__ == '2.5.8'` at benchmark time).

Code has been implemented that installs the specific Triton nightly `3.0.0.post20240424212437` (or a functionally equivalent post-20240424 nightly) so the Triton baseline uses H100-specific instructions as in the paper.
The H100 is placed in a deterministic clock/power state for benchmarking as described in Appendix C.1.

Code has been implemented (typically a shell script invoked before benchmarking) that runs `nvidia-smi -lgc 1830,1830` (or `nvidia-smi --lock-gpu-clocks=1830`) to pin the GPU graphics clock to 1830 MHz, and the failure to do so (e.g. missing root) is surfaced as a warning in the benchmark log.

Code has been implemented that, immediately before each measurement, queries `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=clocks.gr --format=csv,noheader,nounits` and asserts the reading is 1830 MHz (±1 MHz), aborting the run otherwise.

The environment achieves and holds the reported 1830 MHz clock: a smoke run recorded in `results/clock_check.log` shows the sampled clock is 1830 MHz for at least 10 consecutive samples spaced 1 s apart during a matmul workload.
Benchmark timing methodology matches Appendix C.1 (100 repetitions, averaged) and uses sequence-length choices that avoid wave quantization on 132 SMs.
Code has been implemented that runs each attention configuration 100 times (after a warmup phase) and reports the arithmetic mean wall time, matching the paper's protocol.

Code has been implemented so that for sequence lengths ≥ 4096 the benchmark uses lengths divisible by 132 (specifically 4224, 8448, 16896 as noted in Appendix C.2) to avoid wave quantization on the H100's 132 SMs.

Baseline reference implementations exist for standard PyTorch attention, FlashAttention-2 (CUDA), FlashAttention-2 in Triton (H100-tuned), and cuDNN 9 fused attention, callable with identical (batch, seqlen, nheads, headdim, causal, dtype) settings for like-for-like comparison.
A unified Python dispatch layer exposes every baseline attention through a single call signature so downstream benchmarks and error tests can iterate over them without special-casing.

Code has been implemented that defines a common `run_attention(impl, Q, K, V, causal, dtype)` (or equivalent) dispatch function accepting (batch, seqlen, nheads, headdim) tensors and returning the attention output tensor with matching shape (batch, seqlen, nheads, headdim).

Code has been implemented that supports the required precision set on the same call path: FP16 and BF16 for `standard`, `flash2`, `flash2_triton`, and `cudnn`, and FP8 (e4m3) for `standard` (per-tensor scaled baseline) and `cudnn` (where available).

Code has been implemented that enables the `causal` flag on every baseline (standard PyTorch via mask, FA2/Triton/cuDNN via their causal argument) and produces outputs consistent with a strictly lower-triangular attention mask.

For a small (batch=2, seqlen=256, nheads=4, headdim=64) FP16 input with fixed seed, the FP32-reference output of `standard`, `flash2`, `flash2_triton`, and `cudnn` agree with each other to within a max-abs tolerance of 5e-3 (non-causal and causal), verifying interchangeability of the baselines.
A reference standard PyTorch attention that materializes S and P in HBM is available as the 'Standard attention' baseline in Figures 5–7 and the FP8/FP16 baseline in Table 3.

Code has been implemented that computes standard attention as S = alpha * Q @ K^T, P = softmax(S), O = P @ V, materializing S and P as full [N,N] tensors in HBM (no fusion), matching the Section 2.3 definition.

Code has been implemented so that the standard-attention FP16/BF16 path keeps the softmax reduction (max, exp, sum) in FP32 before casting back, matching the paper's description in Section 4.3 that intermediate softmax is FP32.

Code has been implemented for an FP8 (e4m3) standard-attention baseline that uses per-tensor scaling on Q, K, V, an FP32 matmul accumulator, and keeps intermediate softmax results in FP16 — exactly the baseline described for Table 3.
The FlashAttention-2 CUDA baseline is wired to the same dispatch layer and pinned to version 2.5.8 as specified in Appendix C.1.

Code has been implemented that imports `flash_attn` at version 2.5.8 and calls `flash_attn_func` (forward) and `_flash_attn_backward` / autograd (backward) through the common dispatch, with `causal` and `dtype` forwarded correctly.

Code has been implemented that programmatically asserts `flash_attn.__version__ == '2.5.8'` at import (or is version-pinned in the environment file) so benchmarks cannot silently run against a different FA2 build.

Code has been implemented that calls the FA2 baseline on (batch, seqlen, nheads, headdim) shapes with headdim in {64, 128, 256} and FP16/BF16 dtypes, producing an output whose shape and dtype exactly match the input Q shape and dtype.
The FlashAttention-2 Triton baseline (H100-tuned, using Hopper-specific instructions) is available and callable through the common dispatch, matching the 'Triton' curve in Figures 5 and 7 / Figure 9.

Code has been implemented that imports the FlashAttention-2 Triton kernel (from `flash_attn.flash_attn_triton` or the Triton nightly 3.0.0.post20240424212437 tutorial kernel referenced in Appendix C.1) and exposes it via the common dispatch under name `flash2_triton`.

The Triton kernel used as the baseline uses H100-specific instructions (WGMMA / TMA via Triton's Hopper backend or the tutorial kernel tuned for `sm_90a`), and this is verifiable either by the kernel's autotune configs (num_warps/num_stages targeting Hopper) or by a runtime check that it is compiled with `sm_90a`.

Code has been implemented so that a call to `flash2_triton` at (batch=2, seqlen=1024, nheads=8, headdim=64, causal=False, dtype=FP16) runs end-to-end without recompilation errors and returns an output that matches the standard-attention reference within 5e-3 max-abs.
The cuDNN 9 fused attention baseline (the 'cuDNN' curve in Figures 5, 6, 7, and 9) is wired through the common dispatch at cuDNN 9.1.1.17.

Code has been implemented that invokes cuDNN 9's fused-attention API (via `cudnn-frontend` graph API or `torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention` with the cuDNN backend forced on) and exposes it under the common dispatch as `cudnn`.

Code has been implemented that asserts the linked cuDNN version is exactly 9.1.1.17 at import (via `torch.backends.cudnn.version()` or the cudnn-frontend `get_cudnn_version` call), matching Appendix C.1.

Code has been implemented that supports both forward and backward calls on the cuDNN baseline for FP16/BF16 with headdim in {64, 128, 256} and both causal and non-causal masks (needed to reproduce Figure 5, Figure 6, and the cuDNN entries in Figure 9).
Code has been implemented that also supports the cuDNN 9 FP8 forward path (for the FP8 comparison curves in Figure 7 and Figure 9), including passing per-tensor scales for Q, K, V.
A shared benchmark/measurement harness drives every baseline identically so that reported TFLOPs/s across implementations are directly comparable.
Code has been implemented that times each baseline with CUDA events, averages 100 repeats, and reports mean runtime — matching Appendix C.1's protocol.

Code has been implemented (or a script provided) that fixes the H100 SXM5 GPU clock to 1830 MHz via `nvidia-smi --lock-gpu-clocks=1830,1830` (or equivalent) before benchmarking, matching Appendix C.1.

Code has been implemented that computes TFLOPs/s using the paper's formula: forward FLOPs = 4 * batch * nheads * seqlen^2 * headdim (halved when causal), and backward FLOPs = 2.5 * forward FLOPs, then divides by measured seconds.

Code has been implemented that iterates the benchmark grid used in the paper: seqlen in {512, 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192, 16384} (with the ≥4k values snapped to divisibility by 132 for FP8 as in Appendix C.2), hidden=2048, headdim in {64, 128, 256}, batch chosen so total tokens = 16k, both causal and non-causal.

Code has been implemented that gracefully records 'OOM' (rather than crashing the whole sweep) when a baseline runs out of memory at large seqlen, so that partial results are still logged as in Figures 5 and 6.

Algorithm 1 is implemented at the CTA level with a producer warpgroup issuing TMA loads of Q, K, V into an s-stage circular SMEM buffer and consumer warpgroup(s) running WGMMA-based QK^T and PV GEMMs with online softmax rescaling, using setmaxnreg to (de)allocate registers.

The FlashAttention-3 forward CTA kernel launches with a grid parallelized over batch, heads, and Q-tile blocks, and tile sizes B_r, B_c, and head_dim d are compile-time template parameters selected per head dimension.

Code has been implemented that exposes a forward host entry (e.g., mha_fwd) taking Q, K, V tensors of shape (batch, seqlen, num_heads, head_dim) and dispatching a Hopper CUDA kernel whose grid dimensions equal (ceil(N/B_r), num_heads, batch).

Code has been implemented that specializes the kernel by head_dim (64, 128, 256) and by causal vs. non-causal, selecting distinct (B_r, B_c, num_stages, num_consumer_warpgroups) tuples for each specialization at compile time.
Code has been implemented so that at kernel entry each CTA computes T_r = ceil(N / B_r) and T_c = ceil(N / B_c), and iterates key/value blocks 0 <= j < T_c in the mainloop.

A unit test constructs a small forward call, inspects the launched grid via a CUDA event / kernel-info hook, and confirms grid.x == ceil(N/B_r), grid.y == num_heads, grid.z == batch for head_dim 64, 128, and 256.

Warpgroups are split into one producer warpgroup and one or more consumer warpgroups, and setmaxnreg is used to shrink the producer register file and grow the consumer register file at the top of the kernel.

Code has been implemented that assigns each warpgroup a role based on warpgroup_id: warpgroup 0 executes the producer branch (TMA issuer) and warpgroups 1..num_consumer are consumers running WGMMA/softmax; the branch is selected on all threads of the warpgroup.

Code has been implemented that calls cutlass::arch::warpgroup_reg_dealloc<N_producer>() (or equivalent PTX setmaxnreg.dec) inside the producer branch and warpgroup_reg_alloc<N_consumer>() inside the consumer branch, with N_producer < N_consumer.

The chosen producer register count and consumer register count are both multiples of 8 within the range [24, 256] permitted by setmaxnreg, and their weighted sum is consistent with the H100 SM per-CTA register budget for the selected (num_consumer_warpgroups) configuration.

The consumer branch, after reallocation, has enough registers to hold the FP32 O_i accumulator (B_r x d), l_i, m_i (each B_r), and one B_r x B_c FP32 S tile without spilling; a small stress test compiled with -Xptxas -v shows zero register spills for the head_dim=128 configuration.
A pipeline object with an s-stage circular SMEM buffer for K and V (and a separate slot for Q) manages producer/consumer synchronization using mbarrier arrive/wait primitives.

Code has been implemented that allocates s SMEM slots each sized for one K tile (B_c x d) and one V tile (B_c x d), with s a compile-time constant (num_stages) chosen per head-dim configuration and equal to at least 2.
Code has been implemented that allocates a separate single-slot SMEM region for Q_i sized B_r x d and loaded once per CTA (not part of the circular buffer).

Code has been implemented that constructs a CUTLASS PipelineTmaAsync (or equivalent mbarrier pair) with num_stages == s and initializes the producer/consumer thread counts to match the warpgroup role assignment.
Code has been implemented that indexes the buffer stage as (j % s) in both the producer and consumer paths so that the same physical SMEM slot is reused across iterations.
Code has been implemented that after the consumer finishes the PV GEMM for iteration j, calls pipeline.consumer_release(stage=(j%s)) so the producer can overwrite that slot in iteration j+s.

A behavioral test with instrumentation verifies that for the first s producer iterations no consumer_wait blocks are hit (buffer fills without waits), while iteration s and later the producer stalls until stage (s%s) is released by the consumer.
The producer warpgroup mainloop issues TMA loads of Q_i once and of K_j, V_j for each 0 <= j < T_c, committing to the pipeline to notify the consumer.
Code has been implemented that inside the producer branch, on a single elected thread, issues a cp.async.bulk.tensor (TMA) load of Q_i from GMEM into the Q SMEM slot before entering the K/V loop.
Code has been implemented that after issuing the Q TMA, arrives on the Q-load barrier to signal completion of the Q load to the consumer warpgroup.
Code has been implemented that iterates j from 0 to T_c-1 in the producer, and at each iteration first calls pipeline.producer_acquire(stage=(j%s)) which waits for the stage to be consumed.

Code has been implemented that inside each producer iteration issues one TMA load for K_j and one TMA load for V_j into the (j%s)-th slots and commits the transaction bytes to the stage's mbarrier so the consumer's arrive-wait completes.
Only a single warp (or single thread) inside the producer warpgroup issues each TMA (matching Hopper's TMA one-thread issuer semantics); other producer threads only participate in barrier arrival.

A behavioral test using cuda-gdb / a proxy inspection of SMEM contents confirms that after the producer finishes iteration j the SMEM slot (j%s) contains the exact byte pattern of K[j*B_c:(j+1)*B_c, :] and V[j*B_c:(j+1)*B_c, :].
The consumer warpgroup mainloop executes two WGMMAs per iteration (SS-GEMM for QK^T and RS-GEMM for P̃V) interleaved with online softmax rescaling, matching Algorithm 1 lines 14–23.
Code has been implemented that initializes the on-chip state O_i = 0 (B_r x d, FP32), l_i = 0 (B_r), m_i = -infinity (B_r) before entering the consumer mainloop.
Code has been implemented that arrives-and-waits on the Q-load barrier before entering the mainloop so Q_i is guaranteed to be in SMEM.
Code has been implemented that at the top of each consumer iteration j calls pipeline.consumer_wait(stage=(j%s)) so that K_j (and, jointly, V_j) are visible before the WGMMA issues.

Code has been implemented that issues the first WGMMA as an SS-GEMM computing S = Q_i * K_j^T from both SMEM operands, using wgmma.mma_async.sync.aligned with an FP32 accumulator, followed by wgmma.commit_group and wgmma.wait_group.sync 0.

Code has been implemented for the online softmax update: after S is ready, store m_old = m_i, compute m_i = max(m_old, rowmax(S)), compute P̃ = exp(S - m_i) (using the *2 scale trick with the log2(e) constant is acceptable) and l_i = exp(m_old - m_i) * l_i + rowsum(P̃).
Code has been implemented that rescales O_i by diag(exp(m_old - m_i))^(-1) (fused as a multiply by exp(m_old - m_i) into the FP32 accumulator) before accumulating the PV product.

Code has been implemented that issues the second WGMMA as an RS-GEMM (operand A in registers = P̃ after FP32->FP16/BF16 conversion, operand B in SMEM = V_j) that accumulates into O_i, followed by wgmma.commit_group and wgmma.wait_group.sync 0.

The FP32 S tile is converted to the FP16/BF16 precision required by the RS-GEMM's operand-A register layout before being fed to the second WGMMA (e.g., via cutlass::NumericArrayConverter or F2FP PTX), preserving the WGMMA operand fragment layout.
After the second WGMMA completes, the consumer calls pipeline.consumer_release(stage=(j%s)) exactly once per iteration so the producer can refill that slot.
The consumer epilogue finalizes O_i by dividing by l_i, computes the log-sum-exp L_i = m_i + log(l_i), and writes O_i and L_i back to HBM as the i-th blocks.
Code has been implemented that after the mainloop multiplies O_i by 1/l_i in FP32 (broadcast per row) and, only then, converts to the output dtype (FP16/BF16) for HBM writeback.
Code has been implemented that computes L_i = m_i + log(l_i) (or L_i = m_i / log2(e) + log2(l_i) equivalent) and writes L_i to the logsumexp output tensor slot for query block i.

Code has been implemented that writes the FP16/BF16 O_i tile back to HBM via TMA store (cp.async.bulk.tensor store) or an equivalent vectorized STG path into the (batch, head, query-block, head_dim) slot.
The producer/consumer warp-specialized forward kernel is end-to-end correct: it matches a reference attention implementation on synthetic inputs across head dimensions and sequence lengths.

A behavioral test invokes the FA3 forward kernel with random Q, K, V in FP16 for (batch=2, num_heads=8, seqlen=1024, head_dim=64) and asserts max-abs elementwise difference vs. a full-FP32 PyTorch reference of the same attention formula is below 5e-3.
The same test is repeated for head_dim=128 and head_dim=256 (each with an appropriate B_r, B_c) and passes with max-abs elementwise difference below 5e-3 versus the FP32 reference.

A behavioral test with seqlen not divisible by B_r or B_c (e.g., seqlen=1000, B_r=64, B_c=64) confirms the kernel handles boundary Q- and K/V-blocks correctly (residual rows produce identical output to reference within 5e-3).

The returned per-row logsumexp tensor L matches the reference L = m + log(sum(exp(S - m))) computed in FP32 to within 1e-3 absolute error for the (batch=2, num_heads=8, seqlen=1024, head_dim=128) configuration.

A behavioral test disables the pingpong and 2-stage overlap (compile-time flag that selects the pure Algorithm 1 path) and confirms the pure warp-specialized-only kernel still produces bitwise-identical outputs to the overlapped kernel within 1e-3 relative error, isolating the correctness of the Algorithm-1 baseline.

The warp-specialized forward kernel achieves the Algorithm-1-only performance point reported for FP16, head_dim=128 in Section 3.1 (~570 TFLOPs/s at batch=4, seqlen=8448, nheads=16, non-causal, before adding pingpong).

The two-warpgroup pingpong scheduling using bar.sync to overlap softmax of one warpgroup with GEMMs of the other is implemented and delivers the reported ~570 → 620-640 TFLOPS uplift for FP16 forward at head dim 128, seqlen 8192.
The forward kernel has the two-consumer-warpgroup CTA layout required for pingpong scheduling.

Code has been implemented so that the FP16 forward kernel launches two consumer warpgroups per CTA (in addition to the producer warpgroup) — verifiable via the kernel's block-dim / warpgroup count constants or template arguments.

Code has been implemented so that each of the two consumer warpgroups is assigned its own Q tile Q_i (distinct row block) with an independent output tile O_i, so that the two warpgroups process complementary halves of the CTA's query work.

Code has been implemented so that `setmaxnreg` (or its CUTLASS wrapper) reallocates register file for the two-consumer layout — the producer warpgroup releases registers while each consumer warpgroup increases its per-thread register count as documented in the paper's warp-specialization scheme.

Code has been implemented so that the single producer warpgroup issues TMA loads of K_j and V_j into the shared circular SMEM buffer that is consumed by both consumer warpgroups (i.e., producer serves both consumers, not one per consumer).
The `bar.sync`-based scheduling primitives that force interleaving of the two warpgroups' GEMM and softmax phases are implemented.

Code has been implemented so that named `bar.sync` (or `barrier.sync` / CUTLASS `NamedBarrier`) instructions are emitted inside the consumer mainloop of the FP16 forward kernel — verifiable by grepping the source for `bar.sync` / `NamedBarrier::sync` inside the pingpong code path.

Code has been implemented so that the barriers use distinct barrier IDs (or role tags) for warpgroup 1's GEMM-arrival vs. warpgroup 2's GEMM-arrival, so the two warpgroups can wait on the other's phase without deadlocking.

The barrier placement forces warpgroup 1's GEMM0 (QK^T) and GEMM1 (PV) to be issued (WGMMA.arrive) before warpgroup 2's corresponding GEMMs of the same iteration — verifiable behaviorally via a unit test that instruments issue order (or via a SASS/PTX inspection assertion in a diagnostic test).

The barrier placement ensures that while warpgroup 2 is running its GEMMs, warpgroup 1's softmax (rowmax, exp, rowsum) executes on the multi-function unit — verifiable via a scheduling-inspection unit test on a captured trace or via an `assert` on the ordering of `bar.sync` and `MUFU.EX2`-adjacent code sections.
The roles alternate ('pingpong') across warpgroups and iterations as described in §3.1 and Figure 1.
Code has been implemented so that after warpgroup 1 completes its GEMM phase and enters softmax, warpgroup 2 begins its GEMMs (i.e., roles swap within the same tile iteration).
Code has been implemented so that the alternation repeats every KV-block iteration of the consumer mainloop for the full [0, T_c) range, not just the first iteration.

A compile-time flag or template parameter (e.g. `kUsePingpong` / `USE_PINGPONG`) exists that toggles the pingpong path off, so a controlled A/B ablation (pingpong-on vs pingpong-off, same tile sizes) can be run from the same kernel source.
The pingpong-enabled kernel produces numerically correct attention output.

Code has been implemented so that the pingpong FP16 forward kernel's output matches the non-pingpong FP16 FlashAttention-3 forward kernel (same tile sizes, same inputs) elementwise within FP16 rounding tolerance, on a small (batch=1, heads=1, seqlen=1024, hdim=128) test case.
Code has been implemented so that the pingpong FP16 forward kernel's output matches a PyTorch reference `softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d)) V` within RMSE ≤ 5e-3 on random inputs at hdim=128 and seqlen=8192.

Code has been implemented so that two invocations of the pingpong kernel with identical inputs and identical seeds produce bitwise-identical outputs, confirming the barrier-based scheduling does not introduce nondeterminism.

Code has been implemented so that both consumer warpgroups' O_i tiles are correctly written to their respective row-blocks of the output (i.e., no warpgroup's output is silently dropped by the pingpong barriers) — checked by verifying that every row of O has nonzero contribution consistent with the reference on a full seqlen=8192 case.
A benchmark harness exercises the pingpong-on vs pingpong-off configurations at the exact prose-quoted setting (FP16 forward, hdim=128, seqlen=8192) and reports TFLOPs/s.

Code has been implemented so that a benchmark script runs the FP16 forward pass at head_dim=128, seqlen=8192, non-causal, with a batch/heads configuration consistent with the paper (e.g. batch such that total tokens ≈ 16k), and reports TFLOPs/s using the paper's FLOP formula (4·batch·nheads·seqlen^2·hdim).

The benchmark harness pins the H100 GPU clock to 1830 MHz (or otherwise stabilizes clocks) and averages over ≥100 timed iterations after warmup, matching the paper's benchmarking protocol (Appendix C.1).
The measured TFLOPs/s numbers reproduce the paper's prose claim in §3.1: non-pingpong ≈ 570 TFLOPS, pingpong-enabled 620–640 TFLOPS at FP16 forward, head dim 128, seqlen 8192.

With pingpong disabled (but warp-specialization and 2-stage GEMM-softmax pipelining still on), the FP16 forward benchmark at hdim=128, seqlen=8192, non-causal measures approximately 570 TFLOPs/s (within tolerance) — matching the pre-pingpong number quoted in §3.1.
With pingpong enabled, the FP16 forward benchmark at hdim=128, seqlen=8192, non-causal measures in the 620–640 TFLOPs/s range (within tolerance) — matching the post-pingpong number quoted in §3.1.

The measured pingpong-on minus pingpong-off TFLOPs/s uplift at hdim=128, seqlen=8192 FP16 forward is positive and lies in the ~50–70 TFLOPs/s band implied by the paper's 570 → 620–640 statement (within tolerance).

Algorithm 2 is implemented as the consumer path: within a single warpgroup, the second WGMMA (PV) of iteration j is overlapped with softmax computations from iteration j+1, using an extra register buffer for S_next, and the SASS confirms the interleaving matches the expected pattern.
The Algorithm 2 skeleton (prologue for the very first key/value tile, and epilogue for the last tile) is implemented as the FP16 consumer warpgroup path.

Code has been implemented so that on entry to the consumer warpgroup the kernel calls setmaxnreg.inc.sync.aligned.u32 to reallocate the predetermined number of registers as a function of the number of consumer warps (line 1 of Algorithm 2).

Code has been implemented that initializes the on-chip accumulator O_i to zero, the row-sum ℓ_i to zero, and the row-max m_i to -∞ over a fragment of shape B_r × d (line 2 of Algorithm 2) before any WGMMA is issued.

Code has been implemented that waits (via the mbarrier-based pipeline object from Algorithm 1) for both Q_i and K_0 to be resident in shared memory before issuing the prologue WGMMA (line 3 of Algorithm 2).

Code has been implemented that issues S_cur = Q_i · K_0^T as a WGMMA (SS-GEMM), then executes wgmma.commit_group and wgmma.wait_group<0> before touching S_cur (line 4 of Algorithm 2 — this is the only commit-and-WAIT WGMMA in the prologue).

Code has been implemented that, after the prologue WGMMA completes, signals the producer that stage 0 of the K circular SMEM buffer is free (line 5 of Algorithm 2) by arriving on the corresponding empty mbarrier.

Code has been implemented that, before entering the pipelined main loop, computes m_i (row-wise max update), P̃_cur = exp(S_cur - m_i), ℓ_i, and rescales O_i by diag(exp(m_i^old - m_i))^{-1} — the full local-softmax step of line 6 of Algorithm 2 applied to the prologue tile.

Code has been implemented that, after the pipelined main loop, waits for V_{T_c-1} to be resident in SMEM and issues the final O_i += P̃_last · V_{T_c-1} WGMMA with commit AND wait (line 19 of Algorithm 2), i.e. the epilogue PV drains all in-flight WGMMAs.

Code has been implemented for the epilogue (line 20 of Algorithm 2): O_i is rescaled by diag(ℓ_i)^{-1}, L_i = m_i + log(ℓ_i) is computed, and both O_i and L_i are written to HBM as the i-th blocks of O and L.
The overlapped main loop of Algorithm 2 (lines 8-16) is implemented so that the second WGMMA of iteration j and the softmax on S_next (from iteration j+1) are in flight together.
Code has been implemented that, at the top of every main-loop iteration j, waits on the (j%s)th K-full mbarrier for K_j to be resident in SMEM before issuing the QK^T WGMMA (line 8 of Algorithm 2).

Code has been implemented that issues S_next = Q_i · K_j^T as a WGMMA followed by wgmma.commit_group WITHOUT a subsequent wgmma.wait_group, deferring the wait until after the second WGMMA is also in flight (line 9 of Algorithm 2).
Code has been implemented that then waits on the ((j-1)%s)th V-full mbarrier for V_{j-1} to be resident in SMEM before issuing the PV WGMMA of iteration j (line 10 of Algorithm 2).

Code has been implemented that issues O_i += P̃_cur · V_{j-1} as a WGMMA (RS-GEMM, with P̃_cur sourced from registers) and issues wgmma.commit_group without waiting (line 11 of Algorithm 2), so BOTH the QK^T of iteration j and the PV of iteration j are unfinished commit-groups when softmax begins.

Code has been implemented that issues wgmma.wait_group<1> (or equivalent) so that execution blocks only on the QK^T WGMMA of iteration j (S_next), while the PV WGMMA of iteration j is still allowed to be in flight (line 12 of Algorithm 2).

Code has been implemented that computes the softmax update on S_next — the new m_i, P̃_next, and ℓ_i — while the PV WGMMA of iteration j is still executing asynchronously on the Tensor Cores (line 13 of Algorithm 2). This is the overlap the section is about.

Code has been implemented that, after the softmax on S_next completes, issues wgmma.wait_group<0> to drain the PV WGMMA of iteration j and only then applies the diag(exp(m_i^old - m_i))^{-1} rescaling to O_i (line 14 of Algorithm 2).

Code has been implemented that, after the PV WGMMA of iteration j is drained, releases both the (j%s)th stage of the K buffer AND the ((j-1)%s)th stage of the V buffer back to the producer (line 15 of Algorithm 2) via mbarrier arrives.

Code has been implemented that copies (aliases or memcpies at register granularity) S_next -> S_cur and P̃_next -> P̃_cur at the bottom of the loop body so the next iteration operates on the freshly produced values (line 16 of Algorithm 2). The name P̃_cur must always refer to the most recently softmaxed tile.
The pipelined main loop keeps two full S-tile fragments in the register file (S_cur and S_next), matching the section's stated register-pressure trade-off.

Code has been implemented that allocates an extra register-resident tile S_next of shape B_r × B_c and dtype float32, in addition to S_cur, so that consumer register footprint exceeds the non-pipelined baseline by exactly B_r × B_c × sizeof(float) bytes per threadblock.

Code has been implemented so that P̃_cur and P̃_next are held in register fragments across loop iterations (rather than round-tripped through SMEM), enabling the RS-GEMM form of the PV WGMMA required by Algorithm 2 line 11.

A build-time or runtime report is produced (e.g. from ptxas -v or cuobjdump) recording the per-thread register count and any register spills for the 2-stage consumer kernel, so that the paper's register-pressure warning can be checked against reality.
Behavioral tests verify that the 2-stage consumer path is functionally equivalent to Algorithm 1 and that its asynchronous ordering matches the specification.

A deterministic unit test builds a small FP16 attention problem (e.g. batch=1, heads=1, seqlen=256, hdim=128) and asserts that the output of the 2-stage-pipelined consumer kernel matches the output of the non-pipelined Algorithm 1 consumer kernel to within 1e-3 max-abs difference on the same inputs.

A test parses the compiled kernel's PTX and asserts that in the mainloop body there are exactly two wgmma.mma_async instructions, one wgmma.commit_group after each, one wgmma.wait_group with argument >0 (partial drain for S_next), and one wgmma.wait_group<0> (full drain for PV) — matching the Algorithm 2 line 8-16 pattern.

A test asserts that the S_next wgmma.wait_group is issued lexically BEFORE the softmax-on-S_next code block, and the PV wgmma.wait_group<0> is issued lexically AFTER the softmax block and BEFORE the O_i rescaling — the exact partial-drain ordering that makes the 2-stage overlap correct.

The kernel runs to completion without hangs or CUDA errors at the {batch,seqlen,nheads,hdim} = {4, 8448, 16, 128} FP16 non-causal configuration used in the paper's ablation table, so that the section can be exercised at its intended scale.

The SASS-level verification described in Appendix B.2 is reproduced: the disassembly of the FP16 forward kernel confirms that softmax, F2FP conversion, and the first WGMMA's HGMMAs are interleaved as expected.
A script/reproduce step builds the FP16 forward kernel with -lineinfo and extracts the SASS of the consumer mainloop via cuobjdump --dump-sass into a checked-in text file under results/sass/.

A SASS analysis script scans the extracted disassembly for the token classes HGMMA, WARPGROUP.ARRIVE, WARPGROUP.DEPBAR, MUFU.EX2, F2FP, FFMA, FMUL, and FMNMX, and emits a per-region count table that the subsequent assertions consume.

The SASS analysis asserts that at least one MUFU.EX2 / FMNMX / SHFL.BFLY softmax instruction is emitted BEFORE the first WARPGROUP.ARRIVE + HGMMA burst of a mainloop iteration, confirming the compiler reorders softmax to the top of the region as stated in Appendix B.2 observation (1).

The SASS analysis asserts that between the WARPGROUP.ARRIVE and the closing gsb0-tagged HGMMA of the FIRST WGMMA burst, the HGMMAs are interleaved with F2FP.F16.F32.PACK_AB, MUFU.EX2, FADD.FTZ, and FFMA.FTZ instructions (Appendix B.2 observation (2)+(3)).

The SASS analysis asserts that the SECOND WGMMA burst (HGMMA.64x128x16.F32 ... .tnspB, i.e. PV) consists of a contiguous run of HGMMAs with no interleaved F2FP / MUFU / FADD / FFMA instructions, matching Appendix B.2 observation (4).

The SASS analysis asserts the presence of a trailing WARPGROUP.DEPBAR.LE gsb0 (i.e. wgmma.wait_group) at the end of the mainloop region, confirming the drain semantics described in the code listing at the bottom of Appendix B.2.

A results/sass_analysis.md report is produced that lists, for each of the four Appendix B.2 observations, whether the extracted SASS satisfies it (pass/fail with the matched instruction line numbers).
The 2-stage-pipelined consumer path is exposed as a selectable variant of the FP16 forward kernel so downstream ablations can toggle it independently of warp specialization.

Code has been implemented that exposes a compile-time template flag or runtime CLI switch (e.g. --intra-wg-pipeline={on,off}) selecting between the Algorithm 1 non-pipelined consumer and the Algorithm 2 2-stage-pipelined consumer for the FP16 forward kernel.

The benchmark harness invokes the 2-stage-pipelined kernel path when the intra-warpgroup-pipelining flag is on, and records TFLOPs/s and wall time so its contribution is measurable against the non-pipelined baseline of the same kernel.

The 3-stage pipelining variant (Algorithm 4) that additionally overlaps the first WGMMA of iteration j+2 with softmax of j+1 and the second WGMMA of j is implemented and evaluated, reproducing the paper's Appendix B.3 finding that it underperforms the 2-stage variant due to unfavourable NVCC reordering and higher register pressure.

Algorithm 4 is implemented in the forward-pass FP16 kernel as a compile-time selectable consumer variant, with the same producer warpgroup / TMA circular-buffer scheme as the 2-stage kernel and the same {Q,K,V} tile shapes and output contract.

Code has been implemented that exposes a `pipeline_stages=3` (or equivalent template/build flag) selecting the 3-stage FP16 forward consumer path, distinct from the 2-stage path but sharing the same producer warpgroup, epilogue, and public kernel signature.

Code has been implemented for the priming section of Algorithm 4 (lines 2–6): the consumer waits for K0, issues S = Q_i K0^T with a blocking WGMMA, computes m_i, ~P_i, ell_i, scale_o from S, then waits for K1 and issues S = Q_i K1^T with another blocking WGMMA before entering the mainloop.

Code has been implemented for the Algorithm 4 mainloop body (2 ≤ j < T_c − 2) that (a) waits for K_j and issues the first WGMMA S_next = Q_i K_j^T non-blocking, (b) waits for V_{j-2} and issues the second WGMMA O_i += ~P_i V_{j-2} non-blocking, (c) computes m_i, ~P_i_next, ell_i, scale_o from the current S, (d) waits for all previous WGMMAs, and (e) copies S_next→S and ~P_i_next→~P_i, in that order.

Code has been implemented for the Algorithm 4 tail (lines 18–24) that drains the two remaining V tiles: wait V_{T_c-2}, rescale O_i, O_i += ~P_i V_{T_c-2}, recompute softmax from S, then wait V_{T_c-1}, rescale, O_i += ~P_i V_{T_c-1}, followed by the shared epilogue writing O_i and L_i to HBM.

Code has been implemented that allocates the additional per-thread register buffers required by 3-stage pipelining, namely a second S_next tile of size B_r × B_c × sizeof(float) plus a second ~P_next tile of size B_r × B_c × sizeof(input_dtype) and an extra scale_o vector of size B_r × sizeof(float), and the launch config selects a block-size profile (B_r,B_c) that fits within the H100 per-SM register budget for this variant.
Deterministic behavioral checks confirm the 3-stage kernel is numerically equivalent to the 2-stage FP16 kernel and exhibits the expected overlap and register-pressure signature.

Code has been implemented for a unit test that runs the 3-stage FP16 forward on the same {Q,K,V} inputs as the 2-stage forward at hdim=128, non-causal, and asserts the outputs match elementwise to within a fixed FP16 tolerance (e.g., max-abs-diff ≤ 1e-3), confirming Algorithm 4 computes the same attention function.

Code has been implemented that dumps or parses the compiled SASS for the 3-stage consumer mainloop and verifies the Appendix B.3 observation that only the first WGMMA is interleaved with softmax instructions while the second WGMMA (PV) is emitted as a contiguous HGMMA block with no non-WGMMA instructions interleaved.
The 3-stage vs 2-stage ablation is executed under the paper's Section 4.2 configuration and reproduces the paper's finding that the 3-stage variant is slower.

Code has been implemented for a benchmark harness that runs both the 2-stage and 3-stage FP16 forward kernels at {batch,seqlen,nheads,hdim} = {4, 8448, 16, 128} non-causal, using the paper's timing methodology (fixed 1830 MHz clock, ≥100 repeats averaged) and reporting per-config TFLOPs/s to a results file.

The measured 3-stage FP16 forward throughput at {4, 8448, 16, 128} non-causal is strictly lower than the corresponding 2-stage FlashAttention-3 throughput (paper baseline 661 TFLOPs/s), reproducing the Appendix B.3 qualitative finding that 3-stage pipelining underperforms 2-stage.

Results and analysis have been written to the report (e.g., `results/REPORT.md`) that (a) tabulate the 2-stage vs 3-stage TFLOPs/s numbers, (b) attribute the gap to NVCC failing to overlap the second WGMMA with softmax as shown in the SASS analysis, and (c) attribute the block-size reduction to the additional S_next/~P_next register pressure, matching the two causes cited in Appendix B.3.

The FP8 forward path handles the k-major WGMMA operand constraint via an in-kernel LDSM/STSM transpose of V tiles in SMEM, and reconciles FP32 accumulator vs FP8 operand-A register layouts via byte-permute (d0 d1 d4 d5 d2 d3 d6 d7 pattern), with the V transpose scheduled in the shadow of the preceding WGMMAs.

The FP8 kernel identifies and handles the k-major operand constraint imposed by FP8 WGMMA on the second (PV) GEMM, and chooses in-kernel transpose (option 2 in §3.3) over GMEM pre-processing (options 1a/1b).

Code has been implemented so that FP8 WGMMA calls in the kernel require both operands to be laid out k-major in SMEM (contiguous in the inner K dimension), matching the Hopper FP8 WGMMA constraint described in §2.2.

Code has been implemented so that V tiles staged in SMEM for the FP8 PV WGMMA are made contiguous in the sequence length (N) dimension (i.e. mn-major for V^T, k-major for V as the PV B-operand), rather than contiguous in the head dimension as originally loaded.

Code has been implemented so that the TMA load of V from HBM to SMEM uses the head-dimension-contiguous input layout (as V is stored in GMEM) and does not itself perform the sequence/head stride swap.

Code has been implemented so that the FP8 forward path uses option (2), an in-kernel transpose of V tiles inside SMEM, rather than a standalone GMEM pre-processing transpose kernel (option 1b) or a transpose fused into a prior op such as rotary embedding (option 1a).
The in-kernel V transpose is implemented using PTX LDSM (ldmatrix) and STSM (stmatrix) instructions with byte packing to handle FP8's 8-bit entries.

Code has been implemented so that the V-tile transpose is executed by warps in the producer warpgroup rather than a consumer warpgroup, exploiting the register-efficiency of LDSM/STSM to fit within the producer's small register allocation.
Code has been implemented so that the LDSM (ldmatrix) PTX instruction is issued to collectively load a V tile from SMEM into RMEM at a warp-wide granularity of 128 bytes per LDSM.
Code has been implemented so that the STSM (stmatrix) PTX instruction is issued to collectively store the transposed V tile from RMEM back to SMEM at a warp-wide granularity of 128 bytes per STSM.

Code has been implemented so that FP8 (8-bit) V entries are packed two-at-a-time to appear as 16-bit lanes for the LDSM/STSM 8x8 tile view described in the PTX documentation, matching footnote 8 of §3.3.

Code has been implemented so that register movements are performed between LDSM and STSM to split the packed 8-bit pairs, because the transpose variant of LDSM/STSM cannot split packed 8-bit entries; the composed sequence yields a correct tile-wise transpose for FP8.

The in-kernel transpose, when applied to a synthetic V tile with known FP8 values, produces an SMEM layout that matches torch.transpose(V, seq_dim, head_dim) bit-exactly after unpacking, verified by a unit test independent of the WGMMA pipeline.

Code has been implemented so that the resulting transposed V tile in SMEM is directly consumable by an FP8 WGMMA descriptor for the PV GEMM (i.e. the SMEM tile shape, swizzle mode, and leading dimension conform to WGMMA descriptor requirements).

Code has been implemented so that the producer warpgroup, after its setmaxnreg register deallocation, still retains enough registers to hold an entire V-tile-worth of packed FP8 values for the LDSM/STSM transpose round-trip.

The FP32 accumulator layout of the first WGMMA is reconciled with the FP8 operand-A register layout expected by the second WGMMA via a per-thread byte permutation matching the {d0 d1 d4 d5 d2 d3 d6 d7} pattern described in §3.3.

Code models the FP32 accumulator register-per-thread layout matching Figure 3: for rows 0 and 8, threads T0-T3 own the eight entries d0..d7 arranged as {d0,d1},{d0,d1},{d0,d1},{d0,d1} across T0-T3 in the low half and analogous ownership in the high half.

Code models the FP8 operand-A register-per-thread layout matching Figure 4: for rows 0 and 8, threads T0-T3 each own two consecutive 2-entry chunks {a0,a1},{a2,a3} in the low half and {a4,a5},{a6,a7} in the high half, packed as 8-bit values.

Code has been implemented so that CUDA byte-permute (e.g. the PRMT PTX intrinsic or an equivalent __byte_perm call) is used to reorder register bytes when converting the first WGMMA's FP32 accumulator into the second WGMMA's FP8 operand-A layout.

Code has been implemented so that the per-thread byte permutation reorders the 8-entry sequence from {d0,d1,d2,d3,d4,d5,d6,d7} to exactly {d0,d1,d4,d5,d2,d3,d6,d7}, matching the sequence given in §3.3.

Code has been implemented so that the {d0 d1 d4 d5 d2 d3 d6 d7} permutation is replicated over every 8-byte group of the accumulator register file, matching the paper's statement that the permutation is replicated over every 8 bytes.

Code has been implemented so that the FP32 accumulator values are down-converted to FP8 (e4m3) before the byte-permute step, so that the permutation operates on 8-bit lane data and matches the FP8 operand-A layout.
A unit test verifies that applying the implemented byte-permute on a synthetic register file laid out per Figure 3 produces the register file layout of Figure 4 bit-exactly.
Code has been implemented so that the layout conversion uses only per-thread register operations (byte permute) without any cross-thread shuffle instructions, consistent with footnote 9 of §3.3.
The byte-permute of P columns and the corresponding row permutation baked into the in-kernel V transpose are consistent so that the PV WGMMA still computes the correct output tile.

Code has been implemented so that the byte-permute logically permutes P tile columns in the documented pattern (e.g. columns {0,1,8,9} of the original P tile become the first four columns of the permuted P tile).

Code has been implemented so that the in-kernel V transpose emits V-tile rows in the row order matching the P column permutation used by the byte-permute step (row_perm(V) is consistent with col_perm(P)).
A unit test verifies that PV_permuted = P_permuted @ V_row_permuted equals unpermuted P @ V within FP8 quantization tolerance for random FP8 inputs.

Code has been implemented so that the row permutation of V is fused into the STSM store phase of the in-kernel transpose (i.e. the permutation is expressed as SMEM addressing during the transpose write-back, not as a subsequent extra pass over V).
The in-kernel V transpose for iteration j is scheduled by the producer warpgroup in the shadow of the consumer's WGMMAs involving V_{j-1} and K_j, per §3.3.
Code has been implemented so that during the very first iteration (j=0), the V0 tile is transposed after V0 is loaded into SMEM and before the consumer's first PV WGMMA that consumes V0.

Code has been implemented so that for j >= 1, the producer issues the transpose of V_j while the consumer is executing the PV WGMMA on V_{j-1} together with the QK^T WGMMA on K_j, hiding the transpose latency behind these two WGMMAs.

Code has been implemented so that the transpose completion is signalled to the consumer via the same per-stage pipeline barrier that gates the V_j readiness, so the consumer waits on V_j only after the transposed tile is fully written to SMEM.

Code has been implemented so that issuing the transpose from the producer warpgroup does not block consumer WGMMAs (transpose work stays off the consumer critical path, verified by SASS or NCU-observed overlap in the shadow region).
Code has been implemented so that the producer's own pipeline loop respects that the transpose of V_j must complete before the ((j+1)%s)-th stage's V buffer can be reused for a subsequent V tile.
End-to-end numerical correctness of the FP8 forward pass with in-kernel transpose and byte-permute layout reconciliation is validated against reference implementations.

The FP8 forward output for random Q, K, V of shape (batch=2, seqlen=2048, nheads=16, hdim=128) matches a pure-Python reference that manually transposes V and performs the same block quantization within FP8 rounding tolerance (max abs diff <= 5e-2).

Removing the byte-permute step (as an ablation) causes the FP8 forward output to disagree with the reference implementation, confirming the permutation is functionally required for correctness of the PV WGMMA.

Replacing the in-kernel LDSM/STSM transpose with a pre-transposed V in GMEM (option 1b) yields the same FP8 forward output within FP8 rounding tolerance, confirming that the in-kernel transpose is equivalent in numerics to the alternative pathway.

Block quantization (one scalar per Br×d or Bc×d block of Q, K, V, with per-block scaling of S) and incoherent processing (multiplying Q and K by a random diagonal ±1 times Hadamard matrix M in O(d log d), fused with rotary) are implemented for the FP8 forward path.

Block quantization is implemented: Q, K, and V are partitioned into per-block tiles (Br×d for Q, Bc×d for K and V) with one FP32 scalar per block, and the descaling is folded into the on-chip S / P computation so the FP8 forward pass produces correctly-scaled attention outputs.

Code has been implemented that computes one FP32 scale per Br×d block of Q, corresponding to the tile size used by the FP8 forward kernel, and stores it as a per-block scale tensor of shape (batch, heads, num_q_blocks).

Code has been implemented that computes one FP32 scale per Bc×d block of K and per Bc×d block of V, matching the KV tile size used by the FP8 forward kernel, and stores them as per-block scale tensors.

The per-block quantization function derives each block's scale from the absolute maximum of that block against the FP8 e4m3 representable range (448.0), and returns FP8-cast tensors together with the per-block FP32 scales.

Unit tests confirm that dequantizing a Br×d or Bc×d block quantized with the per-block scaler produces a tensor whose max absolute error is at most one e4m3 ULP per block, and that per-tensor quantization on the same block distribution has strictly larger error.

The FP8 forward kernel consumes the per-block scales of Q and K and multiplies each S = Q K^T tile by the product scaleQ_i · scaleK_j before the online softmax, so no additional wall-clock work is added beyond a scalar multiply per tile.

The FP8 forward kernel applies the per-block V scale scaleV_j to the P̃ V accumulator update so that the final O tile is returned in the correct output magnitude, matching the block-quantization derivation.

A behavioral test dequantizes block-quantized Q,K,V, runs FP32 reference attention, and compares against the FP8 kernel with block quantization enabled; the reported RMSE on N(0,1) inputs is strictly lower than the same kernel run with a single per-tensor scale.

Code exposes a public quantize_blockwise API (or equivalent) that can be invoked as a standalone preprocessing step, so that fusion with an outer operation (rotary embedding) is possible without modifying the FP8 kernel itself.

Incoherent processing is implemented: Q and K are multiplied by a random-diagonal-times-Hadamard matrix M along the head dimension prior to quantization, M is applied in O(d log d) time, and the transformation preserves Q K^T so that attention outputs are unchanged in exact arithmetic.

Code has been implemented that samples a random ±1 diagonal signature vector s ∈ {-1,+1}^d for the incoherent-processing matrix M = diag(s) · H, using a fixed seed API so that Q and K use the *same* signature to preserve QK^T.

Code implements an in-place Hadamard transform H_d over vectors of length d that is a power of two (supporting at least d ∈ {64, 128, 256}), producing outputs that equal the naive H · x reference to numerical tolerance.
The Hadamard transform executes in O(d log d) operations via the butterfly recursion (not the d² dense matmul); a unit test asserts the FLOP/element count grows as log2(d) across d ∈ {64, 128, 256}.
Code applies M = diag(s) · H to Q by first sign-flipping along the head dimension using s, then running the Hadamard butterfly, and analogously to K with the same s.
A behavioral test verifies MM^T = I (up to per-column normalization by 1/sqrt(d)) for the constructed transform: applying it to a random vector twice recovers the original within FP32 tolerance.

A behavioral test computes standard FP32 attention on Q,K,V and on (QM), (KM), V for random inputs and asserts the resulting outputs are equal to within FP32 rounding tolerance, verifying that incoherent processing does not change the attention output in exact arithmetic.
The incoherent-processing transform is applied *before* quantization inside the FP8 pre-processing path (i.e., Q ← QM then quantize_blockwise(Q); K ← KM then quantize_blockwise(K)), not after.
V is NOT multiplied by M (only Q and K are), preserving the correct output; a unit test asserts the pre-processing pipeline leaves V unchanged apart from block quantization.

A behavioral test measures the max absolute value of Q entries before and after applying incoherent processing to an outlier-injected input (N(0,1) + N(0,100)·Bernoulli(0.001)); the post-transform max is strictly smaller than the pre-transform max, evidencing the 'outlier spreading' claim.
The Hadamard + sign transform is fused with the rotary embedding pre-processing step so that incoherent processing incurs no extra memory traffic beyond what rotary already does.

Code provides a fused rotary_plus_hadamard kernel (or PyTorch-compilable function) that takes Q, K, cos/sin tables, and the ±1 signature and writes out FP8-quantized, block-scaled QM, KM in a single memory-bound pass.

A behavioral test compares the fused rotary+hadamard+quant path against the unfused reference (rotary, then Hadamard, then quantize applied sequentially in FP32) and asserts numerical equivalence of the FP8 outputs to within one ULP per block.

A microbenchmark reports the wall-clock runtime of the fused rotary+hadamard+quantize kernel and demonstrates it is not more than 1.25× the runtime of rotary alone on the same shape, evidencing that incoherent processing is 'fused ... at no extra computation cost'.

End-to-end FP8 forward accuracy is measured against an FP64 reference on outlier-injected inputs and reproduces the paper's Section 4.3 / Table 3 RMSE ratios that motivate block quantization and incoherent processing.

A driver script reproduces the FP8 accuracy benchmark: Q,K,V are drawn from N(0,1) + N(0,100)·Bernoulli(0.001), attention is computed in FP64 as reference, and RMSE is reported for (a) baseline FP8 per-tensor quantization and (b) FP8 FlashAttention-3 with block quantization + incoherent processing.
The reproduced RMSE of FP8 FlashAttention-3 with block quantization + incoherent processing on the outlier-injected distribution matches Table 3's 9.1e-3 within tolerance.
The reproduced RMSE of the baseline FP8 attention (per-tensor scaling, FP32 accumulator, FP16 softmax intermediates) on the outlier-injected distribution matches Table 3's 2.4e-2 within tolerance.
The reproduced ratio baseline_RMSE / FlashAttention-3_FP8_RMSE is ≥ 2.4 (i.e., matches the paper's 2.6× accuracy improvement claim within tolerance).

The ablation 'no block quant' (incoherent processing on, per-tensor scale only) is reproduced and yields RMSE matching Table 3's 9.3e-3 within tolerance, evidencing that block quantization contributes materially to the improvement.

The ablation 'no incoherent processing' (block quantization on, no Hadamard/sign transform) is reproduced and yields RMSE matching Table 3's 2.4e-2 within tolerance, evidencing that incoherent processing is the primary contributor when outliers are present.

sub_tasks.requirements: Algorithm 3 is implemented with producer, consumer, and dedicated dQ-writer warp roles: dQ local accumulation via a semaphore-atomic add to global dQ, the preprocessing kernel computes D = rowsum(dO ∘ O), and the backward pass respects the s-stage circular SMEM buffer discipline.
The preprocessing kernel that produces D = rowsum(dO ∘ O) is implemented, launched before the main backward kernel, and its outputs match a reference within numerical tolerance.

Code has been implemented that defines a standalone preprocessing CUDA/CUTLASS kernel (e.g., flash_bwd_preprocess.cu or equivalent) invoked by the backward-pass entry point before the main backward kernel is launched.
Code has been implemented such that the preprocessing kernel performs an elementwise (Hadamard) product of dO and O across the head-dim axis for every (batch, head, row) triple.

Code has been implemented such that the preprocessing kernel reduces (rowsum) the elementwise product over the head-dim axis to yield a per-row scalar D of length N and writes D contiguously to HBM as Tr blocks of size Br.

The preprocessing kernel output D matches a torch reference computation (dO.float() * O.float()).sum(dim=-1) for random FP16 inputs (batch=2, heads=4, seqlen=1024, d=64) with max abs error ≤ 1e-2 and RMSE ≤ 1e-3.
The backward kernel dispatches three warp roles - producer, consumer, and dQ-writer - via warp/warpgroup identity, with the register (de)allocations of Algorithm 3 lines 6, 15 in place.

Code has been implemented such that the backward kernel entry function contains a branch on warpgroup_idx (or equivalent) selecting distinct code paths for the producer warpgroup, the consumer warpgroup(s), and the dQ-writer warp.
Code has been implemented such that the producer warpgroup issues a setmaxnreg deallocate (or an equivalent CUTLASS warpgroup_reg_dealloc call) at the start of its role.
Code has been implemented such that the consumer warpgroup(s) issue a setmaxnreg reallocate (or equivalent warpgroup_reg_alloc call) sized as a function of the number of consumer warps.

Code has been implemented such that the backward kernel parallelizes across CTAs over blocks of K/V (i.e., the outer per-CTA index j runs over the Tc key/value blocks and the inner loop iterates over Tr Q/dO blocks), mirroring FlashAttention-2's dK/dV-parallel scheme.

The producer warpgroup issues the K_j / V_j loads once and then iterates over Tr, loading Q_i and dO_i into the (i%s)th stage of the circular SMEM buffer with the correct commit/wait pipeline discipline.
Code has been implemented such that the producer path issues a TMA load of K_j and V_j from HBM to SMEM exactly once (before the inner-i loop) and commits a barrier arrival to notify the consumer.
Code has been implemented such that the producer iterates i from 1 to Tr, issuing TMA loads of Q_i and dO_i into SMEM slots at the (i%s)th stage of the circular buffer.

Code has been implemented such that at each iteration the producer first waits on a pipeline consumer-release barrier for the (i%s)th stage before issuing new Q_i / dO_i TMA loads (empty-slot back-pressure).

The consumer warpgroup implements the full Algorithm 3 inner-loop math over Tr blocks: two SS-GEMMs, the softmax and dS recomputation, the two RS-GEMM dK/dV accumulations, and the dQ_local computation.
Code has been implemented such that consumers wait on the K_j/V_j load barrier once (before the i-loop) and on the Q_i/dO_i (i%s)-stage barrier at each iteration.
Code has been implemented such that the consumer initializes on-chip dK_j and dV_j accumulator tiles to zero before entering the i-loop.

Code has been implemented such that the consumer computes S_ij = Q_i K_j^T using an SS-form WGMMA (both operands in SMEM) and dP_ij = dO_i V_j^T using an SS-form WGMMA, with commit and wait discipline.

sub_tasks.requirements: The Table 2 ablation is reproduced at {batch,seqlen,nheads,hdim}={4,8448,16,128} non-causal FP16: full FlashAttention-3 at ~3.538 ms / 661 TFLOPs, no-pipelining variant at ~4.021 ms / 582 TFLOPs, and no-warp-specialization variant at ~4.105 ms / 570 TFLOPs.
A dedicated ablation benchmark harness targets the exact Table 2 configuration (FP16 non-causal, batch=4, seqlen=8448, nheads=16, hdim=128) and exercises the three ablation variants.

Code has been implemented that exposes a runnable benchmark entry point (e.g., a script such as `benchmarks/table2_ablation.py` or equivalent) that produces the Table 2 numbers for the pipelining/warp-specialization ablation.

Code has been implemented so that the benchmark hard-codes the ablation shape {batch=4, seqlen=8448, nheads=16, hdim=128} (or reads it from a config that defaults to these exact values) and runs in FP16 with no causal mask.

Code has been implemented so that a warmup phase followed by N>=100 timed iterations is used to measure kernel wall time via CUDA events (or equivalently torch.cuda.Event), mirroring the paper's benchmark protocol (100 repetitions averaged).

Code has been implemented that computes achieved TFLOPs/s from measured milliseconds using the standard non-causal attention FLOP count 4 * batch * seqlen^2 * nheads * hdim, so the mapping between the ~3.538 ms and 661 TFLOPs cells in Table 2 is consistent.

Code has been implemented so the benchmark runs at a fixed H100 SM clock (e.g., locks or reports 1830 MHz) and prints, for each variant, both the achieved time in milliseconds and the achieved TFLOPs/s in a format matching Table 2 rows.
The three ablation kernels (full, no-pipelining, no-warp-specialization) are wired up to the same forward attention call so the benchmark selects among them.

Code has been implemented so the full FlashAttention-3 forward variant used in the ablation enables both the intra-warpgroup 2-stage GEMM-softmax pipelining (Algorithm 2) AND the producer/consumer warp-specialization (Algorithm 1) at hdim=128 FP16.

Code has been implemented for the 'No GEMM-Softmax Pipelining, Warp-Specialization' variant: warp-specialized producer/consumer kernel with the intra-warpgroup 2-stage overlap disabled (i.e., the consumer follows Algorithm 1's serialized softmax/GEMM path, not Algorithm 2).

Code has been implemented for the 'GEMM-Softmax Pipelining, No Warp-Specialization' variant: a non-warp-specialized kernel (unified warpgroup with no producer/consumer split) that still performs the 2-stage GEMM-softmax pipelining within the consumer path.

Code has been implemented so all three ablation variants share the same tile sizes (Br, Bc), SMEM stages, and numerical configuration (FP16 inputs, FP32 accumulate) so any measured time difference is attributable to pipelining vs. warp-specialization, not tile-size differences.

Code has been implemented that dispatches to the requested variant via a CLI flag / config key (e.g., `--variant {full, no_pipeline, no_warpspec}`), so a single benchmark invocation can emit all three Table 2 rows.

For each variant the kernel's forward output is numerically checked against a reference attention implementation on the exact ablation shape (max abs error within a small FP16 tolerance) before timing, so a variant that silently miscomputes cannot pass the ablation table by being fast.
The ablation results are produced and recorded as a Table 2-shaped artifact (JSON/CSV/Markdown) with one row per variant and columns for time (ms) and TFLOPs/s.

Code has been implemented so running the ablation script writes a machine-readable artifact (e.g., `results/table2_ablation.json` or `.csv`) containing the three variant labels and their measured `time_ms` and `tflops` values.

Code has been implemented so the ablation script also emits a human-readable Table 2-style rendering (Markdown or plain-text table) with rows labeled 'FlashAttention-3', 'No GEMM-Softmax Pipelining, Warp-Specialization', and 'GEMM-Softmax Pipelining, No Warp-Specialization'.
The three Table 2 numerical claims are measured on H100 SXM5 and land within tolerance of the paper's numbers.

Measured full FlashAttention-3 (both warp-specialization and 2-stage GEMM-softmax pipelining enabled) at {batch=4, seqlen=8448, nheads=16, hdim=128} non-causal FP16 achieves approximately 3.538 ms wall time and approximately 661 TFLOPs/s, matching the Table 2 'FlashAttention-3' row.

Measured 'No GEMM-Softmax Pipelining, Warp-Specialization' variant at the same {batch=4, seqlen=8448, nheads=16, hdim=128} non-causal FP16 configuration achieves approximately 4.021 ms and approximately 582 TFLOPs/s, matching Table 2's second row.

Measured 'GEMM-Softmax Pipelining, No Warp-Specialization' variant at the same {batch=4, seqlen=8448, nheads=16, hdim=128} non-causal FP16 configuration achieves approximately 4.105 ms and approximately 570 TFLOPs/s, matching Table 2's third row.

The measured ordering across the three variants matches the paper: full FlashAttention-3 is fastest, and both single-feature variants (no-pipelining and no-warp-specialization) are slower, confirming that both algorithmic improvements independently contribute to the 570 -> 661 TFLOPs/s speedup claimed in Section 4.2.

The Table 3 RMSE study is reproduced with Q,K,V drawn from N(0,1) + N(0,100)·Bernoulli(0.001) and compared against an FP64 reference: FP16 baseline 3.2e-4 vs FA2/FA3 1.9e-4 (~1.7× lower), FP8 baseline 2.4e-2 vs FP8 FlashAttention-3 9.1e-3 (~2.6× lower), and ablations without block quantization (9.3e-3) and without incoherent processing (2.4e-2).
The synthetic outlier-featured Q,K,V generator, FP64 reference kernel, and RMSE harness that drive Section 4.3 are implemented.
Code has been implemented that generates Q, K, V tensors for the numerical error study at the shapes matching the FP16/FP8 kernels being validated (batch, seqlen, nheads, hdim configurable).

Code has been implemented so each entry of Q, K, V is drawn from N(0,1) plus an independent term drawn from N(0,100) that is multiplied by an independent Bernoulli(0.001) mask, matching the paper's distribution 'N(0,1) + N(0,100)·Bernoulli(0.001)'.
The empirical fraction of entries that receive the outlier N(0,100) contribution is measured on a large sample and lies within a small tolerance of 0.001 (0.1%).
Code has been implemented that accepts a fixed random seed and produces bitwise-identical Q, K, V tensors across repeated invocations so RMSE numbers are reproducible.
Code has been implemented for an FP64 reference attention that computes O = softmax(α·Q·K^T)·V with all matmul, softmax, and rescaling arithmetic carried out in FP64.

The FP64 reference produces an output that, when compared against itself with numerically equivalent formulations (row-wise max subtraction on/off), differs by less than 1e-10 RMSE, confirming the reference itself is numerically stable.

Code has been implemented for an RMSE metric computed as sqrt(mean((O_method - O_ref_fp64)^2)) after casting both tensors to a common floating-point type, applied element-wise over the full output tensor.
The RMSE utility, given two identical tensors, returns 0 (to within FP64 epsilon), and given tensors that differ by a known constant c returns |c|, verifying correctness of the metric implementation.
FP16 attention paths (standard, FlashAttention-2, FlashAttention-3) are exercised through the RMSE harness and produce the paper's Table 3 FP16 row.
Code has been implemented that runs a standard (non-flash) FP16 attention baseline where S and P are materialized and softmax is performed in FP16, so it can be evaluated by the RMSE harness.

Code has been implemented that runs FlashAttention-2 in FP16 (keeping intermediate softmax rescaling in FP32) end-to-end on the synthetic Q, K, V and returns an output tensor consumable by the RMSE harness.
Code has been implemented that runs FlashAttention-3 in FP16 (with FP32 softmax intermediates) end-to-end on the synthetic Q, K, V and returns an output tensor consumable by the RMSE harness.
The measured RMSE of the standard FP16 attention baseline against the FP64 reference on the outlier-featured Q, K, V matches Table 3's 3.2e-4 within tolerance.
The measured RMSE of FlashAttention-2 FP16 against the FP64 reference on the outlier-featured Q, K, V matches Table 3's 1.9e-4 within tolerance.
The measured RMSE of FlashAttention-3 FP16 against the FP64 reference on the outlier-featured Q, K, V matches Table 3's 1.9e-4 within tolerance.
The ratio (RMSE of standard FP16 baseline) / (RMSE of FlashAttention-3 FP16) measured on the same Q, K, V is approximately 1.7×, matching the paper's stated FP16 improvement.
FP8 attention paths (per-tensor baseline, full FA3 FP8, and the two accuracy ablations) are exercised through the RMSE harness and produce the paper's Table 3 FP8 rows.

Code has been implemented for a baseline FP8 attention that uses per-tensor scaling for Q, K, V, keeps the matmul accumulator in FP32, and holds intermediate softmax results in FP16, matching the paper's baseline description.

Code has been implemented for the full FP8 FlashAttention-3 path with both block quantization (per-block scalars on Br×d or Bc×d blocks of Q, K, V) and incoherent processing (random ±1 diagonal × Hadamard multiplication of Q and K) enabled, exercised through the same RMSE harness.

Code has been implemented for the 'no block quantization' ablation configuration of FP8 FA3, in which per-block scaling is replaced with per-tensor scaling while incoherent processing remains enabled.
Code has been implemented for the 'no incoherent processing' ablation configuration of FP8 FA3, in which the Q,K Hadamard/sign multiplication is skipped while block quantization remains enabled.

The incoherent-processing helper produces a random orthogonal M as a product of ±1 diagonal matrices and a Hadamard matrix, and unit tests verify that M·M^T = I (within FP32 tolerance) and that (Q·M)(K·M)^T equals Q·K^T (within FP32 tolerance).

The block-quantization helper produces one scaling factor per Br×d (Q) or Bc×d (K,V) block and unit tests verify that dequantizing a quantized block reconstructs the original tile within FP8 e4m3 quantization error.
The measured RMSE of the per-tensor FP8 baseline against the FP64 reference on the outlier-featured Q, K, V matches Table 3's 2.4e-2 within tolerance.
The measured RMSE of full FP8 FlashAttention-3 (block quant + incoherent processing) against the FP64 reference on the outlier-featured Q, K, V matches Table 3's 9.1e-3 within tolerance.
The measured RMSE of the 'no block quantization' FP8 FA3 ablation matches Table 3's 9.3e-3 within tolerance.
The measured RMSE of the 'no incoherent processing' FP8 FA3 ablation matches Table 3's 2.4e-2 within tolerance.
The ratio (RMSE of per-tensor FP8 baseline) / (RMSE of full FP8 FlashAttention-3) measured on the same Q, K, V is approximately 2.6×, matching the paper's headline FP8 accuracy improvement.

The 'no incoherent processing' RMSE is materially higher than the 'no block quantization' RMSE (roughly 2.5× or more), matching the paper's ordering that incoherent processing contributes more of the FP8 accuracy gain than block quantization.
The numerical-error experiment is packaged as a runnable, self-reporting artifact whose output can be compared against Table 3.

Code has been implemented for a single driver script that sweeps all seven Table 3 configurations (Baseline FP16, FA2 FP16, FA3 FP16, Baseline FP8, FA3 FP8 full, FA3 FP8 no-block-quant, FA3 FP8 no-incoherent) on the same generated Q, K, V and emits an RMSE for each.
The driver writes a machine-readable results artifact (e.g. results/table3.json or table3.csv) containing one row per method with the method name and RMSE, plus the seed and QKV shape used.

The driver also emits a human-readable Table 3 equivalent (Markdown or plain text) grouping FP16 methods together and FP8 methods (baseline, full, no-block-quant, no-incoherent) together, matching the two-panel layout of the paper's Table 3.
